title: Recursion: the Base Case and the Recursive Case
quickIdea: A recursive function is two parts: a case that returns without calling itself, and a case that calls itself on a smaller input. A function with only the second part is not a recursion, it is a loop that never ends.
remember: The base case returns a value without any further call. The recursive case calls the same function on input that is strictly closer to the base case.

Two obligations, both examinable: at least one base case must be reachable from every legal input, and every recursive call must make measurable progress towards it (a smaller n, a shorter string, a halved range).
The structure is induction: the base case is the basis and the recursive case is the inductive step. A proof that a recursion is correct is an induction on the size of the input.
C needs no special syntax. Inside its own body a function's name is already declared, so it may call itself; a forward declaration is only needed when two functions call each other.

Direct recursion is a function calling itself; indirect recursion is a cycle through other functions (f calls g, g calls f). Both are legal C and both terminate only if the argument decreases across the whole cycle.
GATE almost never asks for a definition. It gives ten lines and asks for the output, the number of calls or the return value, so the working skill is the trace, not the vocabulary.

example.prompt: int sum(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return n + sum(n - 1); } What does sum(3) return, and how deep does the recursion go?
example.work: sum(3) = 3 + sum(2); sum(2) = 2 + sum(1); sum(1) = 1 + sum(0); sum(0) returns 0 without a call. The chain is four activations deep, and the additions happen on the way back up: 1, then 3, then 6.
example.answer: sum(3) = 6, with four activations on the stack at the deepest point.

gateAngle: The base case decides whether an answer exists at all: GATE CSE 2019 Q.26 is a program whose base case can never be reached, and the correct option is that nothing is printed and the function never terminates. Every other recursion question assumes the base case works and asks about the trace.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: int fact(int n) { if (n == 1) return 1; return n * fact(n - 1); } What happens when fact(0) is called?
variations.answer: It never reaches a base case: the argument walks 0, -1, -2, ... and the recursion runs until the stack is exhausted.
variations.why: The base case handles the smallest input the author had in mind, not every input the program can be given - the exact failure mode of GATE CSE 2019 Q.26.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Is a base case alone enough to guarantee that a recursion terminates?
variations.answer: No. The recursive argument must move towards the base case. int f(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return f(n + 1); } has a base case and still never terminates for a positive input.
variations.why: Separates the two obligations, which are tested separately: a missing base case in 2019 Q.26, a base case the argument cannot reach in the same question.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Rewrite the sum function so that its base case is n == 1 and it is still correct for n = 0.
variations.answer: Either keep an explicit test for n == 0 returning 0, or start the recursive case at n <= 1 returning n. A single base case at n == 1 is not enough, because sum(0) would then call sum(-1).
variations.why: The distractor in a base-case question is always a base case that is one input short.

trap.what: Assuming that a base case written for the intended inputs protects the function from every input it can actually receive.
trap.why: The recursive case generates the arguments, not the caller. If the generated arguments can step past the base case (into negatives, or to a fixed point that is not the base case), the function loops even though a base case is present.
trap.counterexample: convert(n) in GATE CSE 2019 Q.26 tests n < 0 but recurses on n / 2; from 0 the argument stays 0, so the test is never true and the recursion never ends.

check.question: int f(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return n + f(n - 1); } What does f(-3) do?
check.answer: It recurses for ever (until the stack overflows).
check.explanation: The base case tests n == 0, and the argument only ever decreases, so starting from -3 it never equals 0. A base case must cover every value the recursive case can produce, which is why the safer form is n <= 0.

covers: a recursive definition: smaller copy plus a base case
one frame per call: own parameters, own locals, own return address
nothing is computed on the way down; values combine on the way up
fact(n) and sumTo(n): calls = depth = n+1
the C standard does not require tail call optimisation
static local inside a recursion is one object shared by all frames
